title: Field guide: node evacuation, GPU hot-swap, and rapid cluster recovery (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working runbook for on-call SREs to:
- Rapidly evacuate a node (cordon/drain) with GPUs under load
- Perform a field GPU hot-swap / replacement on bare metal or dedicated hosts
- Recover a cluster to service after multi-node GPU-related incidents
- Add short-term capacity or scale up nodepools when needed

Scope / when to use this doc:
- Use when a node is failing hardware checks (GPU errors, ECC, poor throughput) or kernel messages show GPU faults.
- Use when pods are OOMKilled or failing due to GPU driver faults.
- Use for both Hosted Dedicated racks and Private (on-prem) clusters. For cloud-managed clusters, follow provider-specific control plane docs first, then this for infra-level actions.

TL;DR runbook (order of ops):
1) Assess impact & notify (Slack + PagerDuty)
2) Cordon the node -> drain user-facing pods with safe eviction flags
3) Verify KV cache and model-serving fallbacks (ensure routing policy is active)
4) If hardware: run quick health checks (nvidia-smi, dmesg, IPMI), attempt soft-reboot; if not fixed -> schedule GPU swap
5) Replace GPU with vendor-approved procedure, reseat, power cycle, verify drivers
6) Bring node back: join kube, uncordon, validate running pods and metrics
7) If capacity impacted: add temporary nodes or scale Dedicated pool, enable autoscaler override
8) Post-incident notes + handoff to infra engineering for RCA

Immediate checklist (first 10 minutes):
- Who: oncall -> @pager on Slack, mention eng-sre and solutions-engineering if customer impact.
- Severity: estimate SLO/latency impact and affected customers (use console dashboards)
- Identify failing node(s): kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady / ReadyUnknown
- Check GPU health: SSH to node (if allowed), run nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv
- Look at kubelet logs: journalctl -u kubelet -n 500
- Check DCGM / node-exporter metrics and host GPU exporter metrics

Cordoning + draining (safe defaults we use on prod clusters):
- kubectl cordon <node-name>  # prevents new pods
- kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
Notes:
- --force only when eviction API is problematic (bad kubelet). Consider --disable-eviction if node is in a weird state.
- For model-serving StatefulSets: prefer scale down of replica and rely on routing/rollout config before drain to avoid cold cache storms.
- If pods do not evict: kubectl describe pod <pod> to see PDBs and eviction errors. If PDBs block critical infra, contact product-owner for temporary PDB override.

Quick hardware triage (on-host checks):
- ipmitool chassis status  # for power issues (on-prem)
- dmesg | grep -i nvidia  or journalctl -k | grep -i gpu
- lsmod | grep nvidia  # driver present
- nvidia-smi -q  # look for ECC errors, remapped rows, persistant clock throttling
- cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version
- smartctl -a /dev/sda  # rule out storage issues if pods fail to start
- check driver crash logs: /var/log/nvidia-installer.log or /var/log/messages
Common findings:
- GPU appears but with ECC errors -> probable hardware fault
- nvidia-smi hangs -> driver/kernel panic -> require reboot/hardware intervention
- nvlink errors or PCIe bus errors in dmesg -> reseat or replace GPU

Attempt soft-remediations before swap: (15–30 minutes)
- systemctl restart docker/containerd and kubelet (if safe)
- rmmod nvidia && modprobe nvidia (only under guidance; may disrupt other GPUs)
- Reboot node (soft power cycle) if maintenance window allows: sudo reboot
If soft-remedies fail or hardware faults persist -> schedule swap

GPU replacement (on-prem / dedicated rack) - field swap checklist:
- Pre-checks: ensure you have correct replacement SKU, firmware, antistatic gear, and that cluster control plane is aware of the node being offline.
- Safety: power down the host (follow rack power-off SOP), or place JIS tool in maintenance if hot-swap supported.
- Document serial numbers for replaced GPU and store old GPU in tagged evidence bag. Photograph slot and sticker.
- Physically reseat GPU first if the issue is intermittent (check connectors for dust, PCIe latch).
- If reseat fails -> remove GPU, install replacement, secure bracket, reconnect power cables.
- Power on host, watch IPMI console for POST errors.
- On boot: check BIOS for GPU presence, ensure NVLink (if used) shows correct connections.
- Login: nvidia-smi; verify driver load and health.
- Run small validation job: gpu-burn-lite or stress-ng container for 2–5 minutes to confirm stability.

Bringing node back to cluster:
- kubelet should register node automatically. If not: check kubelet logs and /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf credentials.
- kubectl get nodes | grep <node> -> once Ready, remove cordon: kubectl uncordon <node-name>
- Validate pods: kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>
- Validate model-serving endpoints: hit health-check routes and run a small inference to ensure latency within expected range.
- Validate metrics: check GPU exporter, prometheus rules (gpu_error_count == 0), and alerting cleared.

Rollbacks & safety:
- If node flaps after rejoin, immediate action: cordon again, drain, and set node to quarantined state for manual evaluation.
- If replacement GPU fails validation, re-image node or off-board node to maintenance pool.

Capacity add (short-term) when multiple nodes impacted:
- If in cloud (GKE/EKS/AKS) -> scale nodepool: gcloud container clusters resize / eksctl scale nodegroup or increase autoscaler CPU/GPUs temporarily. Document commands in cluster runbook.
- For on-prem Dedicated pools: enable warm spare nodes in scheduler, power on standby hosts from BMC, and run configuration script to join cluster.
- Consider model-routing: temporarily route requests to Hosted API region or fallback model variant with lower GPU requirements.
- Communicate planned capacity increase to customer success and product owners for any SLA expectations.

Validation after scale-up:
- Confirm new nodes in cluster: kubectl get nodes | grep -E "<new-node-prefix>"
- Confirm autoscaler metrics show decreased unschedulable pods
- Run canary traffic to ensure increased throughput and monitor latency/cost

Post-incident: Incident timeline template (fill during handling)
- t0 (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC): PagerDuty fired -> initial responder -> notes
- t+5m: Initial triage results (nodes affected, severity)
- t+15m: Drain started on nodes A,B -> user impact notes
- t+45m: Hardware triage logs collected -> reboot attempted/failed
- t+90m: Swap completed on node A -> validation results
- t+120m: Node A back in service -> residual issues
- t+6h: Mitigations applied (capacity add, routing changes)
- t+24h: Customer communications sent

Postmortem checklist (short):
- Capture logs: kubelet, container runtime, dmesg, nvidia logs, IPMI/event logs (attach to JIRA)
- Store replaced hardware serials and photos in ticket
- Identify root cause: driver regression, hardware age, thermal event, power-cycling issue
- Action items: hardware procurement, driver pin/upgrade, alert tuning, runbook updates
- Assign owners and ETA for each action item

Runbook gaps & open questions (TODOs):
- Add exact provider commands for each cluster type (GKE/EKS/On-prem) and templated scripts for automatic cordon/drain + validation.
- Standardize GPU health metric thresholds (current alerts are noisy)
- Expand spare node onboarding guide for Private deployments
- Create automation to snapshot model KV cache prior to drain for faster warm-up on reattach

Notes to on-call:
- This doc is intentionally terse. If you are unsure, escalate early.
- Keep short, time-stamped notes in the incident ticket and paste key actions to Slack thread.
- Prioritize customer-facing routes: if model-serving region is impacted, failover is preferred to long drain operations.

Appendix: helpful commands
- kubectl get nodes -o wide
- kubectl cordon NODENAME
- kubectl drain NODENAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
- kubectl uncordon NODENAME
- kubectl describe pod PODNAME -n NAMESPACE
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 500
- sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv
- ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc> -U <user> -P <pass> chassis power status

Contact / escalation matrix:
- On-call SRE -> PagerDuty primary -> eskalate to eng-sre lead (Marcus Chen) -> infra-hardware (Lina Gomez) -> product-support (solutions-engineering)

End of draft.
